pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 8–9y; recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations (e.g. list factor pairs of 24; reorder a product for easier calculation).
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y4 'recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): 4.OA.4 — 'find all factor pairs for a whole number in the range 1–100 … recognize that a whole number is a multiple of each of its factors' (leads into prime/composite); 3.OA.5 commutativity as a strategy.
• Operational details — a factor pair is two numbers that multiply to give a target (24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6). The two skills interlock: commutativity means 3×8 and 8×3 are the SAME pair, so you find pairs systematically and stop when they meet in the middle (avoiding duplicates). Factor pairs are found via known table facts and the ×÷ inverse ('what times what makes 24?'). The mental-calculation payoff: reorder/regroup using pairs (e.g. 25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400). Represent each pair as a rectangle (24 dots as 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6 rectangles) so factors ARE the possible rectangle dimensions — the direct bridge to arrays/area and later to primes (a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle).
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 8): find factor pairs of a small number with an array (12). Tier B (age 8–9): list ALL factor pairs of a number to ~50 systematically, using commutativity to avoid repeats. Tier C (age 9): use factor pairs to simplify a mental calculation and explain why you stop searching at the square root.
bestPractices: Search for factor pairs systematically — 1, 2, 3, … in order, pairing each with its partner — and use commutativity to know you've found them all when the pair 'meets in the middle'.
Represent each factor pair as a rectangle of the target number, so a factor is literally a side length and children see the finite set of rectangles a number allows.
Find factors through known table facts and the ×÷ inverse, reinforcing that factor-finding is division/known-fact work.
Use factor pairs and commutativity as mental-calculation tools (reorder/regroup for easy pairs like ×5×2=×10), not just as a listing exercise.
Seed prime/composite intuition: numbers with only the 1×n rectangle (one factor pair) hint at primes; square numbers have a repeated factor (the square).
keyRepresentations: Rectangle/array for each factor pair — factors as side lengths of all rectangles of that number
Systematic factor-pair list (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6) with the 'meet in the middle' stopping point
Factor 'rainbow' arcs pairing 1–24, 2–12, 3–8, 4–6 — shows commutativity and completeness
commonMisconceptions: Listing 3×8 and 8×3 as different pairs (not applying commutativity), inflating the count.
Missing factor pairs by searching unsystematically, especially the middle ones.
Confusing factors with multiples (factors go INTO the number; multiples are in its times table).
Forgetting 1 and the number itself are always a factor pair.
Not knowing when to stop — continuing past the square root and re-finding pairs in reverse.

learn.summary: Teaching factor pairs and commutativity to 8–9 year-olds: a factor pair is two whole numbers that multiply to a target (24: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6). Commutativity means 3×8 and 8×3 are the SAME unordered pair, so pairs are searched systematically from 1 upward and the search stops when the two factors 'meet in the middle' (near the square root). Each pair corresponds to a rectangle the number can form, which bridges to arrays/area and previews primes (a whole number greater than 1 with only the 1×n rectangle). Factor pairs also pay off as a mental-calculation tool via reordering/regrouping (e.g. 25×16 = 25×4×4 = 100×4 = 400). Manipulable rectangle-building is the core; static diagrams, checking tasks, and Socratic questioning serve distinct supporting roles.

activities.title: Rectangle hunt: build every rectangle of a number
feedback: If a rectangle has gaps, it is not a valid arrangement — the dimensions only count as a factor pair when every counter fills a complete rectangle.
When a learner records 3×8 and 8×3 separately, show the same rectangle rotated: same counters, same two factors, so it is one pair, not two.
If a learner is unsure when to stop, point out that once the two sides of the rectangle cross over (near 4 and 6 for 24), every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one.
With 23, prompt: 'Can you make any rectangle other than a single line? What does that tell you about 23?'
activities.rationale: Building rectangles makes the abstract list a felt, discovered structure, ties factor-finding to arrays/area (the total count equals the number), and lets completeness and the stopping point emerge from running out of rectangles rather than from a memorised rule. Contrast with a prime previews prime/composite ideas. Optional live feedback (logging dimensions, drawing rainbow arcs, rotating a rectangle to show 3×8 = 8×3) makes the mechanism concrete but is not required — paper, tiles, or dots work.
sourceClaims: Representing factor pairs as rectangles/arrays and searching systematically (stopping at the square root) supports completeness and previews prime/composite numbers.
4.OA.4 requires finding all factor pairs for a whole number 1–100 and recognising multiples, leading into prime/composite.
learnerActions: Take 24 counters (or squared paper, tiles, or dots) and arrange them into complete, gap-free rectangles, recording the dimensions of each as a factor pair.
Work systematically: ask 'does 1 fit? does 2 fit? does 3 fit?...' in order, logging each rectangle you can make (1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6).
After making 3×8, try to make 8×3 and observe it is the SAME rectangle turned a quarter-turn — record it as one pair already found, not a new one.
Keep going (5 does not fit; 6 gives 6×4, the same rectangle as 4×6) and notice that no NEW rectangles appear once the two sides meet in the middle; explain why you can stop there.
Repeat with 23 counters and discover only a single 1×23 line forms — a whole number greater than 1 that makes only a single 1×n line is prime.
Draw a 'factor rainbow': arcs pairing 1–24, 2–12, 3–8, 4–6 to show each pair and completeness.
activities.intendedInsight: Factors are the possible side-lengths of all rectangles a number can form; commutativity collapses 3×8 and 8×3 into one pair; a systematic search can stop where the factors meet in the middle because every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one; and a whole number greater than 1 that makes only the 1×n rectangle is prime.

activities.title: Factor pairs as a mental-calculation tool
feedback: Check the regrouping preserves the product: 25×4×4 uses the same factors as 25×16 (because 16 = 4×4), so the answer must match (400).
If a learner cannot find a factor, prompt them to use a known table fact or division: 'what number times 4 gives 16?'
activities.rationale: The curriculum goal names mental calculation explicitly; applying factor pairs to real regrouping connects the skill to its payoff and reinforces factor-finding as division/known-fact work.
sourceClaims: Y4 pupils recognise and use factor pairs and commutativity in mental calculations.
learnerActions: Rewrite a multiplication by regrouping convenient factors: turn 25×16 into 25×4×4, then compute 100×4 = 400.
Find a factor pair that makes a product easy (e.g. pairing ×5 with ×2 to make ×10), and explain why reordering is allowed.
Find factors using known times-table facts and the multiplication/division inverse: 'what times what makes 24?'
activities.intendedInsight: Commutativity (changing the order) and regrouping (choosing which factors to multiply first, e.g. 25×(4×4) = (25×4)×4) let you use factor pairs to turn a calculation into easier steps, so factor-finding is a practical mental-maths tool, not just a listing exercise.

activities.title: Prove the list is complete (systematic-search reasoning)
feedback: If the justification is 'I think that's all', model checking each counting number in order from 1 up to the point where the factor pairs meet (e.g. 1 to 6 for 36), recording each result so completeness is demonstrated, not guessed.
For the odd-count question, show that a square's two equal factors (5×5 for 25) count as one factor, so the total is odd.
activities.rationale: A Socratic 'how do you know?' exchange can build the systematic-search and completeness habit and targets the 'stop too early' and 'don't know when to stop' errors. It works alongside, not instead of, the visual rectangle work.
sourceClaims: Representing factor pairs as rectangles/arrays and searching systematically (stopping at the square root) supports completeness and previews prime/composite numbers.
learnerActions: List all factor pairs of a number such as 36, then explain how you know none is missing.
Respond to a challenge — 'Have we found them all? How do you know?' — by describing your sweep from 1 and your stopping point.

Explain why 24 has an even count of factors (8) but a square number like 25 has an odd count (3: 1, 5, 25), because one pair uses the same factor twice (5×5, the square root), so that factor is counted only once.
activities.intendedInsight: Completeness comes from a systematic sweep that pairs each small factor with its partner and stops where they meet, not from feeling finished; in a square number, one pair uses the same factor twice (e.g. 6×6 for 36), so that factor is counted once and the number of factors is odd.

activities.title: Check and sort: factors, pairs, and multiples
feedback: 24 has four distinct factor pairs. If a learner answers eight, they are counting reversed versions (8×3 as separate from 3×8) — these are the same pair.
If a learner lists a multiple (e.g. 48) as a factor of 24, remind them a factor goes INTO 24; a multiple is 24 times something.
Always include 1 and the number itself (1×24) — these form a pair every whole number has.
activities.rationale: Short checkable tasks can verify the duplicate/commutativity and factor-versus-multiple distinctions. A sort or fill-in checks classification but does not itself build the rectangle intuition or elicit the hands-on discovery of the stopping point, so it best follows the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: 4.OA.4 requires finding all factor pairs for a whole number 1–100 and recognising multiples, leading into prime/composite.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing factor pair of 36 given a partial list.
Sort numbers into 'factor of 24', 'multiple of 24', 'both' (24 itself) or 'neither' to distinguish the two ideas.
State how many DISTINCT factor pairs 24 has (four: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6), treating each unordered pair once.
activities.intendedInsight: Factors divide into the number while multiples lie in its times table; distinct factor pairs are counted once because commutativity makes reversed versions the same pair.

constraints: Count a factor pair once: 3×8 and 8×3 are the same unordered pair. The common error of listing them separately (giving 24 '8 pairs') must be corrected in teaching, not presented as a valid option.

Checking/sorting tasks verify understanding and check classification; they do not by themselves build the rectangle intuition or let a learner discover the meeting-in-the-middle point, so they are well placed after hands-on exploration (not a universal requirement).

A static factor-rainbow diagram is a useful reference and can show completeness and commutativity, but it does not let the learner search for pairs or discover the meeting-in-the-middle point themselves.

Physical counters, tiles, or dots have slight thickness and stand in for the ideal flat rectangle; treat the arrangement as a representation of the number's structure where side-lengths = factors and the total count = the number — this legitimately bridges to arrays and area, so preserve (do not deny) the array/area interpretation.
Factor pairs are planar (two factors, rectangles). A three-factor/volume (cuboid) treatment belongs to a different topic and should not be introduced here.
Always include the 1×n pair; every number has 1 and itself as a factor pair.
The 'one rectangle = prime' observation applies only to whole numbers greater than 1; 1 forms only 1×1 but is not prime.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original materials describe stopping 'at the square root'. For these learners this is framed concretely as 'the two sides of the rectangle meet in the middle'; the exact square-root rule is the underlying reason and can be stated by older/more confident learners.
Source claims for CCSS-M 4.OA.4 and the NCETM guidance were marked unverified in the original row; do not treat them as independently confirmed.

The original counted 24 as having four distinct factor pairs; one legacy error-pattern distractor stated '24 has 8 factor pairs' — this is included only as a misconception to correct, never as a correct answer.

The original framed primes as 'numbers with just one rectangle'; this converse is inaccurate for 1, so the learner-facing wording was qualified to whole numbers greater than 1 while keeping the correct direction (a prime makes only the 1×n rectangle).

probeDeeper: How did you know 5 is not a factor of 24?
You wrote 3×8. Is 8×3 a different pair or the same one — why?
How did you know when to stop checking numbers?
24 has an even number of factors but 25 has an odd number. Why might that be?
assess.correctAnswer: 1×24, 2×12, 3×8, 4×6 (and their commutative partners 24×1, 12×2, 8×3, 6×4, which are the same pairs). A child reasoning well works UP from 1 checking each number in turn, stops when the factors meet in the middle (after 4×6, since 5 doesn't divide 24 and 6 has already appeared), and uses commutativity to know 3×8 and 8×3 are one pair, not two.

errorPatterns.pattern: searches unsystematically and stops early — lists 1×24, 2×12, 4×6 and misses 3×8, with no way to know a pair is missing
errorPatterns.nextMove: model checking every counting number in order (does 1 go in? 2? 3? …) and recording each result, so completeness comes from the systematic sweep, not from feeling done.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child offers an incomplete set and, asked how they know it's complete, says 'I think that's all' with no method

errorPatterns.pattern: counts 3×8 and 8×3 as two different factor pairs, inflating the list — not treating commutativity as making them one pair
errorPatterns.nextMove: show 3×8 and 8×3 as the same array rotated a quarter turn — same rectangle, same factors; a factor PAIR is one unordered pair.
errorPatterns.distractor: 24 has 8 factor pairs (3×8 and 8×3 are different)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child lists eight 'pairs' and treats reversed versions as new

errorPatterns.pattern: does not know when to STOP — keeps testing numbers past 24 or is unsure why the search ends, missing that factors pair up around the square root
errorPatterns.nextMove: point out that once the two factors in a pair cross over (here after 4 and 6), every larger factor has already appeared as the partner of a smaller one, so the search is complete.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child keeps trying numbers like 7, 9, 10 aimlessly or asks 'how far do I go?'

responseLevels.gap: finds a few pairs by trial with gaps, no method for completeness, and/or double-counts commutative reversals.
responseLevels.full: sweeps systematically from 1, uses commutativity to pair factors and avoid duplicates, stops correctly where factors meet, and justifies that the list is complete.
responseLevels.partial: finds all four pairs but only by luck or exhaustive guessing — cannot justify completeness or explain the stopping point; may still treat reversals as distinct.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Find ALL the factor pairs of 24 — every pair of whole numbers that multiply to make 24. When you have them, tell me how you knew you had found them all and hadn't missed any.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Unsystematic children find some pairs and guess they are done; the reason tier ('how do you know you have them all?') separates a random search from a systematic sweep up to the square-root turning point. Whether they double-count 3×8 and 8×3 reveals if commutativity is being used to organise the search.
